planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallow, tops exposed, in late summer to fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this striped-leaf sport is grown chiefly as a foliage accent, so give it a spot where the leaves stay visible all season rather than tucking it behind taller neighbors.

directions: Unlike the plain gray-green foliage of the species, 'Variegata' carries bold lengthwise stripes of creamy yellow down each sword-shaped leaf, making the clump ornamental for foliage alone long before or after bloom. In late spring it sends up fragrant, soft blue-lavender flowers scented of grape or orange blossom, held above the striped fans on stems to over 3 feet. This cultivar has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its combination of reliable bloom and season-long variegated interest. Treat exactly like the species for culture: shallow planting, sharp drainage, and full sun keep the stripes crisp and the rhizomes rot-free; it is markedly more of a specimen or edging plant than the plain species, which is grown more for fragrance and historic orris-root use.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant shallow rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this white-flowered selection performs in the same dry-shade and rooftop-type conditions that make the species so unusual among irises.

directions: Where the species blooms lilac-blue with a dark-veined crest, 'Alba' produces pure white, ruffled, orchid-like flowers marked only with fine yellow veining on the crests and falls, giving it a cleaner, more luminous look against shaded foliage. Bloom runs from mid-spring into late spring on flattened stems held just above the low, broad fans of ribbed, semi-evergreen leaves, and clumps spread slowly outward to 2-3 feet wide over time. It shares the species' rare tolerance for dry shade and thin, fast-draining soil — including the ability to grow on old sod or thatched-roof-type plantings — making it a standout white-flowered option for a shaded rock garden or woodland edge where most iris would refuse to bloom. Deer- and drought-tolerant once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright indirect light; the cream-and-green striped leaves scorch in hot, unshaded sites, so give this selection more shade than the plain green species needs.

directions: 'Aphrodite' replaces the species' plain evergreen leaves with fans of crisp cream-and-green striped foliage, so it earns its place as much for season-long variegated groundcover as for bloom. In spring it carries the same delicate, fringed, orchid-like lavender-and-white flowers spotted yellow and orange at the base of the falls, but on a more compact plant than the running species clumps. Distributed by the Italian nurseryman Carl Sprenger as early as 1907, it has long been noted by growers as more vigorous and more strongly marked than older variegated forms of Iris japonica. Use it as a shade-garden accent or container specimen where its striped leaves can be appreciated up close, keeping soil evenly moist through the growing season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, poor, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil at the base of a warm, south-facing wall in full sun; resist the urge to enrich the soil or divide often, since this iris flowers best when starved and left undisturbed for several years.

directions: 'Mary Barnard' was collected in Algeria in 1937 and has become one of the strongest-flowering named forms of the Algerian winter iris, producing rich, deep violet, sweetly scented blooms from midwinter into early spring above narrow, grass-like evergreen leaves. It is noted for being an unusually vigorous, free-flowering grower compared with the variable seed-grown species, holding the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for reliability in the garden. Unlike spring- and summer-blooming irises in this dataset, it flowers in the depths of winter, making it a rare source of fragrant color in the coldest months for gardeners in mild-winter climates. Give it the driest, sunniest, most neglected spot available — rich soil or excess water produces lush leaves at the expense of flowers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil against a warm south- or west-facing wall in full sun; like other named forms of this species it blooms best when the soil is poor and dry and the rhizomes are left undisturbed.

directions: 'Walter Butt' bears large, pale silvery-lavender flowers, sometimes described as orchid-colored, that are noticeably softer and paler than the deep violet of 'Mary Barnard', and it tends to open its first fragrant blooms earlier, from late autumn into winter. Named for the English gardener who selected it, it shares the species' preference for lean, dry, alkaline soil and a hot, sheltered position, where it will flower for months through the coldest part of the year. Its narrow, grass-like evergreen foliage stays tidy through winter, and the pale flowers show up well against dark evergreen backdrops in a winter border. As with other Algerian iris selections, avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, or excess winter moisture, all of which favor leafy growth over bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Careless Sally Siberian Iris (Morgan Award-Winning Ruffled Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; this cultivar can rebloom later in the season if kept consistently watered after its main flush.

directions: Where most Siberian iris cultivars in this dataset are solid-colored selfs, 'Careless Sally' is a multi-tone blend of rose, blue, and lavender in ruffled, heavily textured petals with a bright yellow blotch at the base of each fall, giving individual flowers a watercolor-washed look rather than a clean single hue. Each stalk carries 3 to 5 blooms in midseason and the plant may put out a partial rebloom later in summer under good conditions. It was honored with the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2003, the society's highest award reserved for Siberian iris. At a compact 2 feet tall, it is shorter and denser than taller cultivars like 'Flight of Butterflies', making it useful toward the front of a mixed perennial border.

common_name: Flight of Butterflies Siberian Iris (Small Multi-Bloom Dark Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun; give this taller cultivar extra spacing and, if the site is windy, a bit of support, since its slender stems carry an unusually high number of small flowers per stalk.

directions: Rather than the large, broad flowers typical of most Siberian iris selections, 'Flight of Butterflies' produces unusually small, dark blue blooms patterned with fine white veining on the falls, carried three or more to a stem so that a mature clump in bloom genuinely resembles a cloud of small butterflies hovering above the foliage. It is also later-blooming than most cultivars in this dataset, flowering in July into August rather than late spring, which extends the Siberian iris season in the border. At 30 to 36 inches, its slender upright stems are among the taller Siberian iris forms, making it a good back-of-border or cut-flower selection rather than an edging plant.

common_name: Super Ego Siberian Iris (Morgan Award-Winning Pale Blue and Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; this vigorous cultivar forms large clumps quickly and benefits from division only once it becomes noticeably crowded, typically after 4-5 years.

directions: 'Super Ego' is a bicolor Siberian iris, showing pale sky-blue standards held above noticeably darker violet-blue falls, a two-toned contrast that sets it apart from solid-color selfs like 'Caesar's Brother' in this dataset. Its large flowers open in late spring to early summer on sturdy stems above vigorous, quickly bulking clumps of narrow foliage. It received the American Iris Society's Morgan Award, the society's top honor reserved exclusively for Siberian iris, in recognition of its exceptional flower size and garden performance. Its vigor makes it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for gardeners wanting fast-establishing color at a pond edge or in a moist perennial bed.
